lines: Casey Morgan
+1 (555) 010-7731 | casey.morgan@example.com | example.com/portfolio/cmorgan
Date of birth: 3 Mar 1997 | Nationality: Canadian
EDUCATION
Lakeshore University | B.A. in Cognitive Science | Metro City, USA | Sep 2015 - May 2019
EXPERIENCE
Pinegrove Financial | Senior UX Researcher | Metro City, USA | Mar 2022 - Jun 2025
- Cut the card-dispute form's abandonment rate from 37% to 22% in a four-week A/B test by splitting it into three short steps with saved progress.
- Brought the design system to WCAG 2.1 AA by setting body-text contrast to at least 3:1 against every background.

- Synthesizing 60 interviews, 400 survey responses and 18 months of support tickets through affinity mapping, journey mapping and a tagged clip library, cut repeat support calls about statements by 23%.
- Presented quarterly findings to the head of product and two design teams; three of the top five recommended fixes shipped in the next release cycle.
- Trained 12 product managers to run their own unmoderated tests with a shared script template, which doubled the number of tests run each quarter.
- Led research on the mobile onboarding flow, testing three prototypes with 24 new customers; the shipped design raised completed sign-ups from 41% to 58% in the quarter after launch.
Northwind Health | UX Research Associate | Metro City, USA | Jul 2019 - Feb 2022
- Raised the patient app's Net Promoter Score from 6.1 to 8.4, calculated as the average 0-10 recommendation rating across 2,000 monthly survey responses.
- Interviewed 40 patients about appointment reminders; the findings led to a two-way text reminder that cut missed appointments from 14% to 9%.
- Writes the screener and consent templates for all patient studies, cutting study setup time from two weeks to three days.
- Tested the telehealth waiting-room screens with 16 older patients; the revised layout cut support calls about joining a video visit by 30%.
PROJECTS
Accessible Transit Map | Independent Project | Figma | Sep 2024 - Present
- Redesigned a city transit map for screen-reader and low-vision riders, and tested it with 12 participants on timed route-finding tasks.
- Cut median route-finding time from 90 to 60 seconds, a 50% improvement, by adding audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
- Raised task success by 20% across 12 participants, from 65% to 85%, with audio landmarks and high-contrast line colors.
Community Clinic Booking Redesign | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Figma | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Redesigned a free clinic's online booking flow, cutting the steps to book from 9 to 4; phone bookings fell by a quarter in the next two months.
- Recruited 10 clinic patients and ran two rounds of hallway testing, fixing the six issues that stopped first-time users from finishing a booking.
- Wrote the clinic's volunteer handbook for maintaining the booking pages, which two later volunteer teams used to add Spanish-language booking.
SKILLS
Tools: Figma, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA), Tableau
Methods: moderated and unmoderated usability testing, interveiws, surveys, A/B testing

items.says: Date of birth and nationality are included in the résumé.
items.because: They can invite irrelevant or legally sensitive judgments and take attention away from qualifications.

items.says: Education appears before the professional experience and project evidence that should lead the résumé.
items.because: After roughly six years of work, recruiters are more likely to look first for current UX research experience.

items.says: Setting body-text contrast to 3:1 does not bring ordinary body text into WCAG 2.1 AA compliance.
items.because: Normal-sized body text requires at least 4.5:1 contrast; 3:1 applies only to sufficiently large text.

items.says: The line does not establish what portion of the design system was tested or how compliance was confirmed.
items.because: “Against every background” does not show which components, themes, or color combinations were covered.

items.says: “Brought the design system to WCAG 2.1 AA” claims broader compliance than the contrast change described.
items.because: Readers may interpret it as full design-system compliance.

items.says: The line incorrectly credits synthesis and documentation methods with reducing repeat support calls.
items.because: Those methods organize evidence; a reduction requires an intervention and comparable before-and-after measurements.

items.says: The awkward present-participle opening buries the 23% result after too many inputs and methods.
items.because: “Synthesizing ... cut” is grammatically awkward, and the long list makes the outcome harder to find.

items.says: The stronger outcome—three of five recommended fixes shipping—comes after the presentation details.
The doubled quarterly testing volume lacks its underlying baseline.
The mobile-onboarding bullet leads with a responsibility and puts the sign-up increase after the research details.
items.because: A scanning reader may miss the strongest evidence of impact.

items.says: The line mislabels an average recommendation rating as Net Promoter Score.
items.because: NPS uses the percentages of promoters and detractors, not the average of 0–10 ratings.

items.says: The line does not identify the action or research contribution behind the score change.
items.because: The result reads like a product metric rather than evidence of the candidate’s work.

items.says: The survey-method explanation interrupts the result.
The line does not identify the patient insight that guided the two-way reminder.
items.because: Readers cannot tell how the interviews became a product decision.

items.says: The missed-appointment reduction lacks a comparison period or population.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether the rates cover comparable groups or time windows.

items.says: “Writes” conflicts with the role’s past dates.
items.because: It makes the bullet’s timing unclear.

items.says: The 30% support-call reduction lacks a baseline and comparison period.
items.because: Without an original volume and follow-up period, readers cannot check the change’s size or comparability.

items.says: The phrase describing the support-call outcome is cumbersome.
The first project bullet gives neither an accessibility outcome nor what the test showed.
items.because: It stops at activity despite measurable outcomes in later bullets.

items.says: Calling a reduction from 90 to 60 seconds a 50% improvement is mathematically incorrect.
items.because: The 30-second reduction is 33.3% of the 90-second baseline.

items.says: The project’s strongest outcome is not its opening bullet.
The method phrase repeats the one in the preceding outcome bullet.
The task-success increase is inaccurately labeled “by 20%. ”
items.because: The change from 65% to 85% is 20 percentage points, or about a 30.8% relative increase.

items.says: The booking-flow bullet gives outcomes without showing how the redesign was carried out.
items.because: It does not connect the design work or Figma to a decision or flow change.

items.says: The claim that six issues stopped first-time users generally overstates what testing 10 patients establishes.
items.because: The testing can identify issues encountered by participants, not establish that exactly six issues prevented first-time users generally from booking.

items.says: The bullet does not say whether fixing the six issues improved completion.
items.because: Without a post-fix result, it shows diagnosis and intervention rather than outcome.

items.says: “Hallway testing” may be unclear to a general résumé reader.
The handbook’s relationship to the later Spanish-language addition is unclear and cumbersome.
items.because: The specific guidance or process it enabled is only implied, making the result sound loosely causal.

items.says: Tableau is listed without experience or project evidence showing its use.
items.because: Recruiters cannot tell whether it is a practiced skill or an unsupported keyword.

items.says: “interveiws” is misspelled.
items.because: The visible typo can make the résumé look insufficiently checked.
